projects.name: Immediate Stabilization and Recovery in Cabo Delgado Province, Mozambique
projects.description:
Since 2017 the Province of Cabo Delgado in Mozambique has been facing an escalating conflict, including armed violence compounded by terrorism and connections to extremist cells in East Africa and the confluence of various economic interests in the Mozambique Channel, the occurrences of socio-economic inequalities and expectations related to the exploitation of natural resources, especially among local youth and the perception of political exclusion, and few economic opportunities, affecting in particular young people, consecutive climatic shocks, and recurrent disease outbreaks. Currently, at least  1.5 million people are in need of urgent humanitarian aid1.  It is estimated that in November 2021, over 735,000 internally displaced people were located in relocation camps or informally hosted by communities across the Provinces of Cabo Delgado, Nampula, and Niassa. 

According to the Northern Resilience and Integrated Development Program (PREDIN), by the end of September 2021, attacks resulted in the loss of life of more than 2,000 citizens and forced the displacement of more than 817,000 people.   

Violent attacks by insurgents have significantly heightened protection risks, especially for women and girls. The government of Mozambique, with the strengthening of regional and international cooperation in the field of defense, including with the arrival of troops from the Republic of Rwanda and the SADC Standby Force (SAMIM), reclaimed a number of areas which had been occupied by insurgents. Prior to the arrival of the first Foreign troops on the ground in July 2021, UNDP had initiated stabilization interventions to assist the government of Mozambique in its efforts to re-establish the presence of the State in the reclaimed areas, paving the way for reconstruction and a subsequent safe and voluntary return of IDPs to their areas of origin. UNDP is already working in the districts of Macomia, Quissanga, Mocimboa da Praia and Palma. Benefiting from decades of experience in stabilization activities elsewhere on the continent and in the world, and with an office fully established in Pemba in 2021, UNDP is well positioned to support the government in three interrelated and complementary dimensions as part of stabilization: 

OUTPUT 1: Community security is improved with a focus on Rule of Law and Access to Justice, creating the foundation for social cohesion, peace and development  

OUTPUT 2: Basic services and infrastructure are rehabilitated, functional, and accessible and the capacity of local authorities are developed to improve access to service delivery 

OUTPUT 3: Socio-economic support is provided to individuals and communities, including immediate livelihood support for affected populations 

The support provided by UNDP is aligned with PREDIN's vision to restore and consolidate peace and promote sustainable socio-economic development in the Northern Region of Mozambique, particularly with its pillars 1 (Restoration and consolidation of peace and security) and 3 (Recovery, Reconstruction and socio-economic development and resilience). 

While humanitarian support continues to be provided to populations across the province of Cabo Delgado, the stabilization interventions of UNDP are meant to increase basic state service delivery capacities in areas where security has been restored to allow for the safe return of populations. UNDP supports immediate return of State presence in conflict-affected areas through rehabilitation of damaged infrastructure and institutional capacity building for the restoration of basic services as fundamental conditions for socio-economic recovery. UNDP will ensure a conflict-sensitive, human rights-based and gender-sensitive approach through its response to build forward better, laying the foundations for peace and rule of law, as emphasized by PREDIN.  

UNDP’s stabilization engagement in Mozambique is part and parcels of the Government’s priorities in Cabo Delgado, as embodied in the reconstruction plan (PRCD), and contributing to the Northern Resilience and Integrated Development Program (PREDIN). Along those lines, the present programme is fully integrated with other components of UNDP cooperation in country, as part of its new 2022-2026 programme cycle, with particular complementarity with UNDP’s decentralization programming, as well as with its social cohesion and peacebuilding work. 

UNDP’s stabilization engagement is also grounded in two of the foundational elements of UN wide engagement on internal displacement in which UNDP is called on to a critical role: on the one hand, the 2011 decision on Durable Solutions adopted by the UN Secretary-General, and the accompanying Preliminary Framework on Ending Displacement in the Aftermath of Conflict; on the other hand, the recommendations of the report of the United Nations Secretary-General’s High-Level Panel on Internal Displacement, released in September 20212. As such, the proposed programme builds on the call for development and peace actors to predictably and coherently engage as early on as possible on solutions for displacement. Although it should not be understood as a  peacebuilding intervention, stabilization is conceived as responding to the immediate and critical step on the way to building and sustaining peace, as part of the humanitarian, development and peace engagement (HDP Nexus). UNDP will ensure it engages adequately as part of the existing humanitarian and wider coordination platforms, and will work with sister agencies on the ground.

projects.name: By 2026, girls, boys and adolescents, and their families and communities have increased knowledge and awareness and are better equipped to prevent violence and harmful practices
projects.description: Harmful social norms continue to take a heavy toll on child protection efforts in Mozambique. The prevention of violence through the promotion of positive social norms and behaviour change is a slow process that requires long term commitment and steady engagement with a wide range of partners and with communities, families, adolescents and children. The implementation of the VAC school-based referral mechanism is a landmark achievement and the roll-out of the operational plan to implement the mechanism will be a priority in the new Country Programme, working across sectors, under the leadership of the Education team.  Work with C4D, will focus on triggering behavioural change with and within communities, addressing harmful effects of social (and negative gender) norms and practices that act as socio-cultural barriers towards positive social change. Initiatives will aim to break the culture of silence that continue to hamper reporting and denunciation of acts of violence committed against children, including child marriage. A wide range of Communication for Development methodologies and tools will be developed and used to ensure a multi-level, multi-sectoral, participatory and inclusive social change process, using gender-transformative approaches to ensure gender differences and inequalities are addressed. Activities for prevention of violence and harmful practices will comprise of two inter-connected pillars: social behaviour change communication and parenting skills. Close collaboration  with social protection will ensure that vulnerable children and families do not fall through the social safety.

projects.name: Empowering displaced affected communities – scaling up the eco-system approach
projects.description: In displacement settings, internally displaced persons (IDPs) face significant challenges due to limited access to cooking fuel, lighting, electricity, and other essential energy services. This lack of energy access exacerbates hardships, increases risks of gender-based violence (GBV), puts strain on nearby host communities, and threatens local environmental ecosystems. While the humanitarian sector is beginning to prioritize sustainable energy access, data on current access levels remains scarce. Most displaced individuals in camps rely heavily on traditional biomass for cooking and have negligible or no access to electricity. IOM project aims to address these critical issues by scaling up the implementation of efficient cookstoves, integrating nature-based solutions, and expanding solar energy systems. By doing so, we seek to provide more reliable and sustainable energy sources, thereby reducing dependency on traditional biomass. This approach not only improves energy access but also allows displaced individuals greater dignity and flexibility in choosing their energy solutions.

projects.name: Humanitarian Response in Cabo Delgado, Mozambique (Phase III)
projects.description:
In response to the acute needs of displaced and vulnerable migrants in Cabo Delgado, IOM is currently implementing a comprehensive and integrated Health, WASH, CCCM, DTM, MHPSS, and Shelter intervention. The overall objective of the ongoing project is to ensure dignified, safe, and secure living conditions and access to essential services for populations affected by disasters driven by natural hazards and conflict, while contributing to empowered and resilient individuals and communities across northern Mozambique. This intervention forms part of IOM’s broader multi-donor, multisectoral humanitarian response in the region, which has reached an estimated 784,319 IDPs as of February 2022.

The project is being implemented within the framework of the Humanitarian–Development–Peace Nexus (HDPN), aimed at reducing overall vulnerability, decreasing unmet needs, strengthening risk management capacities, and addressing the root causes of fragility and displacement. Through this integrated approach, the project simultaneously responds to urgent humanitarian needs while supporting recovery, resilience-building, and pathways toward durable solutions. Please note that while the project is operational until March 2027, for the purposes of the current CF submission, the end date will be set as 31 March 2026

projects.name: Strengthening community policing activities and border security systems
projects.description: Cabo Delgado in northern Mozambique has been significantly impacted by a severe context over the past seven years, driven by the Non-State Armed Groups (NSAG) linked to the Islamic State. This violence resulted in the displacement of over 720 thousand people, with many fleeing to neighboring provinces and across borders into Tanzania. The insurgency has been marked by brutal attacks, including beheadings, kidnappings, and destruction of infrastructure, causing widespread fear and trauma among the local population. Allegations of human rights abuses by security forces have further eroded trust between communities and authorities, with concerns that heavy-handed responses may push more people toward supporting the insurgents. IOM’s proposed project focuses on strengthening community resilience, improving border management, and enhancing law enforcement capacity in Cabo Delgado. The project will work on three main fronts: 1) establishing community structures that link to law enforcement, creating a two-way information-sharing system; 2) building trust between law enforcement and communities through positive engagement and capacity-building; and 3) upgrading police stations and border crossing infrastructure to boost operational capacity and security. By adopting this integrated approach, the proposed project aims to contribute to effective and inclusive law enforcement services by creating a collaborative environment where safety concerns can be effectively addressed, bridging communication gaps and enhancing community engagement.

A crisis modifier is included in the Action to respond to a potential crisis that increases humanitarian needs as a result of a natural hazard or other shocks, including epidemics and disease outbreaks. projects.name: Empowering Displaced Communities through Energy Mesh Network
projects.description: IOM Mozambique is attempting an ambitious and innovative initiative of empowering displaced communities through energy in the central provinces of Mozambique. Recognizing the critical need for sustainable energy solutions for Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) in Mozambique, the project aims to revolutionize energy access through a groundbreaking approach. Traditional delivery models have yielded minimal impact and scale, prompting the exploration of more frugal innovations driven by the communities themselves. The project introduces a pioneering model that places the IDPs at the core of the solution development process, empowering them to actively participate in crafting and implementing sustainable energy solutions. This approach not only addresses immediate energy challenges but also ensures the longevity of impact by fostering community-led innovations. The project's focal point is to create an ecosystem where the IDPs are not passive beneficiaries but active contributors to the development and maintenance of the Energy Mesh Network. By championing a community-centric and innovative model, the project seeks to not only improve energy access but also empower displaced communities to take ownership of their energy solutions, fostering sustainability, reliability, and affordability for all.

projects.name: A Health System Strengthing Approach to Tackling Occupational Health Challenges by Migrant Workers - Integrating Occupational and Migrant Health into National Health System (no 4)
projects.description:
Over the past seven years, IOM has developed a tailored approach to address the unique characteristics and needs of migrant mineworkers and farmer workers in Mozambique and South Africa.

IOM has partnered with the Ministry of Health (MISAU) and the Ministry of Labour (MITSS) to address the specific diagnostic and care needs of migrant mineworkers, particularly in relation to TB and HIV. This collaborative effort has involved activities such as follow-up of miners' household contacts in Mozambique and facilitating care and treatment for Mozambican miners in South Africa through cross-border referrals. Additionally, systematic screening centers have been established in Ressano Garcia on the border with South Africa since September 2018.

Since May 2020, IOM, in partnership with MISAU and collaboration with MITSS, has been implementing the project 'Tackling Occupational Health challenges faced by Mozambican miners and migrant workers'. This initiative includes comprehensive Occupational Health screening and counselling services at the Ressano Garcia Occupational Health Centre (OHC). In June 2021, two additional pre-existing OHCs in Gaza province (Xai-Xai and Mandlakazi) were integrated into the project. Through these efforts, IOM has supported the Government of Mozambique (MISAU and MITSS) and Mozambican miners in documenting occupational health conditions and accessing compensation mechanisms by providing regular and quality data on occupational diseases diagnosed in screened migrant workers.

To ensure the sustainability of advancements made in preventing and detecting occupational illnesses among migrant worker populations across southern provinces of Mozambique (Maputo, Gaza, and Inhambane) and cross-border partnerships established under the 'Tackling Occupational Health Challenges' project, IOM provided technical assistance to the Government of Mozambique in 2023 to implement a phased transition. This transition aimed to integrate the project into the national health system by ensuring continuity of service provision at OHCs, strengthening national capacity in occupational health diagnosis, streamlining data collection and reporting mechanisms, and supporting coordination of cross-border partnerships and referral mechanisms. National health system staff have been integrated in the operation of the Occupational Health Centers, and further integration is required or MISAU to take on the operation of the OHCs.

Furthermore, mobile clinics have been deployed to reach remote areas and provide essential healthcare services to migrant workers. Additionally, IOM has collaborated with the Thsiamiso Trust to ensure that migrant workers receive compensation for occupational lung diseases as part of their efforts to support access to justice and fair treatment for migrant workers.

Despite efforts including allocation and training of government human resources, the complete transition did not materialize by December 2023 as initially planned. Critical positions remain unfilled, hindering progress. Additionally, planned sourcing of essential materials and infrastructure maintenance by MISAU in Q3 2024 has not commenced.

Moving forward, IOM aims to support MISAU in developing a long-term sustainable model for providing quality occupational health services for miners and other migrant workers. This endeavor aligns with national strategies for building and strengthening Occupational Health in Mozambique.

Financial compensation from schemes like the MBOD and Tshiamiso Trust fund not only supports affected individuals but also their families, providing stability and healthcare access. With only 9 years left for the Tshiamiso Trust fund, urgent efforts are needed to locate and screen eligible beneficiaries, ensuring ill ex-miners receive rightful compensation. Additionally, families of deceased miners require attention. Through tailored health services and strengthened healthcare systems, IOM aligns with Mozambique's commitment to inclusive healthcare, as outlined in the Government's Five-Year Program (PQG) 2020-2024 and the SDG agenda.

projects.name: Facilitating Cross Border Mobility and Small-Scale Cross Border Trade through Implementing a Mobile Border Pass System along Mozambique/Malawi Borders
projects.description: Malawi and Mozambique are countries of origin, transit, and destination for different categories of migrants and goods. Trade, migration, and cross-border human mobility are inherently interconnected; without people, the vast majority of goods and services would be unable to cross borders and contribute to economic development. In the case of border communities, the link between people and goods becomes unavoidable in the totality of the cases. As Malawi, Mozambique, and the African Union (AU) Member States move towards the implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Agreement (AfCFTA), the importance of effective border management policies increases as countries require measures that facilitate and expedite the movement of persons, goods, and services across borders while ensuring that important security concerns are addressed. Free Movement Protocols promulgated by the Regional Economic Communities (RECs), such as the Southern African Development Community (SADC) Protocol on the Facilitation of Movement of Persons, set out a series of measures related to a facilitated border management approach, which include visa liberalization, travel documentation, border residency arrangements among others aimed at simplifying and facilitating trade between and amongst neighbouring countries within the region and continent. In this regard, facilitating regular cross-border movement to promote trade is key for the achievement of Malawi’s and Mozambique’s development priorities. As part of efficient border management, it has a positive impact on trade, as trade agents, from small-scale traders to multinational companies, will benefit from swift, transparent, and well-organized processes at border posts (BP) and therefore, trade agents might be encouraged to increasingly use the Trade Corridors with efficient border management in place or individual men and women might be encouraged to engage in cross-border trade. This strongly contributes to increased revenues for the respective governments, creates job opportunities and contributes to economic development in general.

projects.name: Promoting gender-inclusive empowerment and social cohesion in displacement-affected communities in northern Mozambique
projects.description:
For over six years, northern Mozambique has faced attacks by Non-State Armed Groups (NSAG) allegedly linked to the Islamic State, resulting in widespread displacement and a complex crisis with dire humanitarian implications. Among the Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) in the country—545,870 out of a total of 721,348—women and girls are disproportionately affected, facing heightened risks of gender-based violence, exploitation, and barriers to accessing essential services. The Northern provinces, where the majority of IDPs are located, struggle to support 55% of these individuals hosted in communities, while over 600,000 persons have returned to their places of origin, often to areas with inadequate infrastructure and limited resources.
To address this, IOM applies a Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus (HDPN) approach to this complex crisis in Northern Mozambique. Through the HDPN, IOM simultaneously responds to the direct humanitarian needs that emerged as a result of conflict and displacement and seeks to address the drivers of conflict and related displacement effects.

With this intervention, IOM will support selected displacement-affected communities by providing them with multi-sectoral assistance, enhancing their resilience and social cohesion, promoting women’s empowerment and gender equality, and facilitating their access to durable solutions in collaboration with a Japanese non-governmental organization (NGO), Peace Winds Japan, in Mocimboa da Praia.

projects.name: Bridging Borders for Women Entrepreneurs in Trade Corridors in Mozambique
projects.description: Serving as a critical trade and mobility route along the border between Mozambique, Malawi and Zambia, the Nacala corridor plays a key role in the region's economic development, income growth and employment creation. The corridor serves an important trade route, including for Informal Cross-Border Trade (ICBT) which is a heavily feminized economic activity. Evidently, informal cross-border trade is important to national economies and livelihoods in the SADC region. Despite its potential for fostering economic diversification and growth through intra-regional trade and investment, women engaged in small-scale cross-border trade (SSCBT) face significant challenges that hinder their economic activities and jeopardize their safety. These challenges include limited access to finance, inadequate infrastructure, and cumbersome border procedures, compounded by widespread corruption and gender-based discrimination. These aspects not only hamper their economic activities but also expose them to risks of sexual assault, exploitation, harassment as well as health risks at border crossings. Other major challenges include inefficiency of customs and immigrations procedures and the lack of proper infrastructure and facilities at border crossing points. The project has three components, contributing to the overall objective of providing integrated support to enable safe and prosperous cross-border trade at the Zobué Border Cross Point, thereby promoting gender-inclusive economic growth.

framework.name: STRATEGIC PRIORITY AREA  1: HUMAN DEVELOPMENT
framework.description: This area aims to contribute to Mozambique’s priority to develop human capital and social justice. It encompasses addressing gaps in gender equality, people’s equitable access to health, nutritious food, WASH, quality education and learning, and social protection, particularly for women and youth, people with disabilities, people and communities in the most vulnerable and marginalized situations, including by addressing harmful practices and gender norms.

children.name: Outcome 1: By 2026, more people, particularly the most vulnerable and marginalized, have a more equitable access to and utilization of quality, inclusive, resilient, gender- and shock-responsive social protection and essential social services.
children.description: This outcome is a concrete commitment of the UN in Mozambique to leaving no one behind and empowering people in line with the national and global targets of SDGs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. It will also contribute to inclusive growth (SDG 8), reduction of inequalities (SDG10) and greater resilience (SDG 11).

children.name: Output 1.1: Mechanisms and capacities of community actors and institutions, including in refugee and IDP hosting areas, to address discriminatory gender and social cultural norms, and prevent and respond to violence and harmful practices are strengthened.
Output 1.2: Vulnerable and marginalized people, including refugees and IDPs, are empowered to access and utilize essential social services and protection systems they need, across the life course

Output 1.3: Capacities of national systems including domestic financial capacity and institutions to deliver human rights-based, people centered, comprehensive essential social services and protection systems for all are enhanced.
Output 1.4: Policy, regulatory and legal frameworks to enhance access and utilization social and protection services are improved.

framework.name: STRATEGIC PRIORITY AREA  2: ECONOMIC DIVERSIFICATION AND SUSTAINABLE LIVELIHOODS
framework.description: This area aims to contribute Mozambique’s priority to boost economic growth, productivity and job generation. It focuses on pursuing an accelerated shift towards more diversified, sustainable and inclusive economic growth, with increased and equitable opportunities for decent jobs and livelihoods and increased incomes, especially for women and youth, people with disabilities and displaced, the most vulnerable and marginalised.

children.name: Outcome 2: By 2026, more people, particularly women and youths, participate in and benefit from a more diversified, inclusive, and sustainable economic growth based on increased production, productivity, and greater value-added chains.
children.description: This result reflects the commitment of the UN to supporting sustainable and inclusive economic development to foster prosperity in Mozambique. Progress in this area would contribute to reducing monetary and multi-dimensional poverty (SDG 1, 2, 10) in addition to putting the economy on the path of sustainability (7, 8, 9, 12) through stronger partnerships (SDG 17).

children.name: Output 2.1: Legal frameworks targeting productive capacity, competitiveness, infrastructure, trade and investment, information and communications are strengthened, gender sensitive and include the needs of refugees and IDPs, and new digital technologies are inclusive and more accessible.

Output 2.2 More people, including refugees and IDPs, especially women and youths, have improved access to income generation opportunities, technical and vocational education and training, and financial and business development and extension services.
children.description: The capacity of young women to access decent work and economic autonomy opportunities increased (SN 2.1.4)

children.name: Output 2.3 The primary sector is more sustainable, productive, value-adding and inclusive of forcibly displaced persons and incorporating circular, regenerative and gender transformative practices.

framework.name: STRATEGIC PRIORITY AREA  3: CLIMATE RESILIENCE AND SUSTAINABLE USE OF NATURAL RESOURCES
framework.description: This area aims to contribute to Mozambique’s priority to strengthen sustainable management of natural resources and the environment. It focuses on accelerating actions on climate change mitigation and adaptation as well as disaster resilience. It prioritises improving the sustainable management of natural resources to enhance the resilience of infrastructure and human settlements and improve national productivity and GDP. It pays special attention to women and youth, people with disabilities, the most vulnerable and marginalised, and their rights to access information, participation and justice in environmental matters, as per Principle 10 of the Rio Declaration.

children.name: Outcome 3: By 2026, more people, especially the most vulnerable, are resilient to climate change and disasters, and benefit from more sustainable management of environment and natural resources and resilient infrastructures and human settlements, with positive effects on national GDP.
children.description: Through this result, the UN recognises both the urgent need for action to improve resilience to disaster shocks and climate change, and the synergies between planet, prosperity and people. children.name: Output 3.1: Policies, strategies, laws and regulations for the use of environmental & natural resources, climate and disaster resilience are developed and strengthened based on good practices and standards and are gender transformative and include the needs of refugees and IDPs.

Output 3.2: Government institutions have stronger capacities for evidence-based (including gender analysis) decision making, accountability, and effective coordination for disasters and climate resilience, resilient infrastructures and the sustainable management of environment and natural resources ;

Output 3.3: Governmental and non-governmental organizations, including forcibly displaced led organizations, have effective and inclusive tools to enhance productivity and revenues through improved sustainable management of environment and natural resources, climate and disaster resilience, and value chains for environmental and natural resources, goods and services.

framework.name: STRATEGIC PRIORITY AREA  4: PEACEBUILDING, HUMAN RIGHTS AND INCLUSIVE GOVERNANCE
framework.description: This area aims to contribute to Mozambique’s priorities to strengthen democracy and national unity, promote good governance and decentralisation, and enhance international cooperation with special attention to women and youth, IDPs, people with disabilities, the most vulnerable and marginalised. It encompasses promoting peace and greater social cohesion through more inclusive, participatory and accountable governance and institutions for people to enjoy their human rights and access an equitable and fair justice system.

children.name: Outcome 4: By 2026, more people, especially the most vulnerable and marginalized, are protected, enjoy their rights, and benefit from a secure, peaceful environment, enabled by inclusive governance systems, and independent and accountable institutions abiding by the rule of law.
children.description: The result engages the UN to support national actors in strengthen their ability to achieve peace and SDG 16, a more equitable society (SDGs 5, 10), and SDG 17, which are critical enablers for the rest of the 2030 agenda.

children.name: Output 4.1: More people, especially the most vulnerable and marginalized and those affected by conflict, including refugees and IDPs, are empowered to actively participate in and lead conflict prevention, community-led stabilization, social cohesion, peacebuilding, and recovery initiatives

Output 4.2: State institutions and decentralized governance bodies are inclusive and have strengthened capacities and policies to operate in line with national, regional and international standards, to ensure rights-based, gender transformative, transparent, and accountable governance;

Output 4.3: Communities, civil society organizations including those led by women and youth, the private sector, and oversight bodies have enhanced capacities to participate in and monitor inclusive governance processes, particularly in areas affected by conflict and disasters.
